article:
In the summer of 1542, a starving Dominican friar floated down a river no European had ever descended, keeping notes. Gaspar de Carvajal was the chaplain of Francisco de Orellana's accidental expedition — a few dozen men in a makeshift brigantine who had set out to find cinnamon and ended up crossing South America by water. What he recorded was not wilderness. [His chronicle describes populous riverbank settlements running for leagues, storehouses of food, travelled roads leading inland, fine ceramics, and organized polities — alternating with stretches he reports as empty]{claim=AMZ-C001}.

For most of the twentieth century, educated opinion held that he was lying, or at best embellishing. The Amazon of the textbooks was a “counterfeit paradise”: soils too poor, protein too scarce, floods too brutal for anything beyond small shifting villages. An eyewitness account of crowded riverbanks was an embarrassment to be explained away — a friar magnifying marvels for patrons back home. And later travelers, arriving a century and more afterward, found mostly what the textbooks predicted: forest, and silence.

This case is about what happens when the instruments catch up with the argument — and about the discipline required to say precisely how much of the friar's world they have found.

## Five ways to read the friar

Set the serious readings side by side, because the evidence below sorts among them unevenly.

- **Invention.** Carvajal made up or grossly inflated a world that never existed; the Amazon could not have supported it. This predicts no large contact-era settlements along his route and no independent witnesses to them.
- **A murdered world.** Carvajal described faithfully what he saw; epidemics, slave raids, missions, and flight destroyed and scattered it before the next visitors arrived. This predicts dense contact-horizon archaeology in his populated reaches and documented collapse mechanisms operating specifically on riverbanks.
- **The garden Amazon.** The whole basin — interfluves included — was densely peopled and intensively managed, by many millions. This predicts intensive-use signals nearly everywhere the soils are cored.
- **The mosaic.** Dense, engineered corridors and hotspots set in a lightly occupied forest matrix; Carvajal is qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable. This predicts strong signals near rivers and bluffs and weak ones in the deep interfluves.
- **The modest skeptic.** Real societies, but smaller than the eyewitnesses imply; Orellana travelled the richest corridors, archaeology looks where it can see, and the emptier later Amazon partly records a modest reality rather than only a collapse. This predicts that population models fall apart under their own assumptions and that the negative record holds up under better sampling.

The first reading has a traceable origin, told below, and has not survived in the form it began. The other four are live, and the question of proportion — how much corridor, how much matrix — is what separates them.

## The account, and its two texts

Before weighing Carvajal against archaeology, there is a problem inside the text itself. His chronicle survives in two main manuscript families, and they do not say the same things. [The most famous numbers — 50,000 warriors, 10,000, 8,000, villages four and five leagues long — appear in the Medina/Muñoz branch but not in Oviedo's version, which preserves the same crowded world with one figure of about 5,000 warriors]{claim=AMZ-C002}. Whatever else is true, the extreme figures are textually unstable in a way the qualitative picture is not.

The two texts are not, however, two independent witnesses. [Oviedo states that he supplemented the friar's written account with particulars he learned orally in Santo Domingo from Captain Orellana and the gentlemen who came with him]{claim=AMZ-C074}. So where Oviedo's text differs from the other branch, the difference may be the friar's own revision, a copyist's, or the captain's memory — and the record does not yet say which way the numbers travelled: whether they grew in one line of copying or were trimmed in the other. What the branch comparison establishes is instability, not direction; the passage-by-passage collation this case calls for below is what would fix it, and the comparison it presently relies on is a geographer's, verified from a scanned copy. Whichever way it ran, a serious reading of Carvajal was never “believe him” or “dismiss him”; it is: trust the kind of world he described, refuse his arithmetic.

### Where the charge of invention began

The oldest accusation on record was not about crowded riverbanks. [Medina, editing the chronicle in 1894, records that the historian López de Gómara cited Orellana's own relación of the voyage and called it “mentirosa” — lying]{claim=AMZ-C068}, and [Medina reads that charge as aimed at the affirmation that Amazons lived on the river]{claim=AMZ-C069}, the episode that gave the river its name. The captain's narrative, not the friar's, drew the word; the marvel, not the towns, provoked it. Two further facts from the same edition frame how the friar has been read since. [Antonio de Herrera's official history follows Carvajal's chronicle “almost to the letter”]{claim=AMZ-C077}, so later Spanish narratives of the voyage are redactions of the same text, not fresh witnesses. And the endorsements are of the man rather than the matter: [Oviedo vouches for the friar on the strength of his two arrow wounds]{claim=AMZ-C072}, [Carvajal himself closes with the genre's protestation that all he has written is true]{claim=AMZ-C075}, and Medina, granting the account “complete faith” limited to the events of the voyage, enters two caveats — [that the friar at times attributes events to supernatural causes]{claim=AMZ-C076}, and that he is an enthusiastic admirer of his captain and countryman. None of this tests a single observation. It tells a reader what the friar's reputation rests on, and where the doubt started.

What does test the observations is other eyes. [A Portuguese named Diogo Nunes had raided the same Machiparo province four years before Orellana, and the ten surviving accounts of the 1560 Ursúa expedition independently describe dense settlement, maize stores one chronicler called infinite, long straight roads “in the manner of the Incas of Peru, except for the walls,” and ceramics of famous quality]{claim=AMZ-C003} — on the same reaches, from witnesses writing for different crowns who were not copying one another. None of them repeats Carvajal's giant numbers. All of them repeat his world. A 2018 study takes a third route to a similar verdict, checking the chronicle's geographic reference points and league distances against the river, and [judges the manuscript a trustworthy historical source]{claim=AMZ-C065}; this record has read only its abstract, which says nothing about the figures. Two limits travel with all of this: fortifications and organized warfare are not among the features the witnesses share, and the route itself is still argued — [one river in Carvajal's itinerary is glossed in the recovered literature with an explicit question mark]{claim=AMZ-C024}, a point held here on its anchor alone.

## What the lasers found

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P01}

The modern turn begins when researchers notice geometric ditches emerging from deforested pasture in the Brazilian state of Acre — and accelerates when LiDAR, which strips the canopy off the terrain model, goes looking under the trees. The survey program led by Martti Pärssinen and Alceu Ranzi has published its reckoning: [flying 4,430 kilometers of laser lines, it documented 432 earthworks where satellite imagery had found a fraction of that, and projects roughly 24,000 to 30,000 monuments across a 183,000-square-kilometer cultural region]{claim=AMZ-C004} — more, for one corner of the basin, than a 2023 basin-wide model predicts remain undiscovered in all of Amazonia.

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P02}

Three honesty notes belong here. First: the study proposes a peak population of 1.25 to 3 million people — but [that figure is an assumption engine, resting on how many earthworks were in use at once and on about 300 people per monument, and the paper's own alternative reading of the same data yields roughly 250,000 to 600,000]{claim=AMZ-C005}. The monuments are certain; the census is a model. Second, and larger: the Aquiry florescence is dated to roughly AD 100–300. It is decisive evidence that Amazonian environments could carry monument-building societies — and weak evidence about what Orellana saw fourteen centuries later. This case refuses to spend ancient grandeur as contact-era corroboration. Third: the 2023 model, built from earthworks known before this LiDAR campaign, estimates 10,272 to 23,648 undiscovered earthworks across all of Amazonia and places nearly all of its highest-probability cells in a 94,713-square-kilometer rectangle over Acre. The two studies define “earthwork” differently and use different data, so the comparison contradicts nothing; it does show that published totals differ several-fold between models, and that only a survey chosen blind to promise can tell which is calibrated.

**Transparency.** The 2026 study's funding statement reads, in its own words: “The project and data collection were funded by a grant from E. Jhong (USA).” That is this site's founder. The Athanatos Foundation, with which he is associated, is acknowledged for administrative assistance. Readers should know this — and should notice that it is exactly why this case presents the paper's population claim at its most assumption-exposed, not its most headline-friendly.

What matters for Carvajal is the archaeology whose dates overlap him. [An 1,800-kilometer arc of the southern rim was occupied by earth-building societies in fortified villages around AD 1250–1500]{claim=AMZ-C006}, with its own population model — half a million to a million — stated as a model that depends on every site being lived in at once. And [several major settlement systems ran into the contact era and beyond: the Belterra Plateau sites near Santarém from about AD 1300 to seventeenth-century colonization, complete with dark earths, ponds, and trodden roads; Marajó's Cacoal site to 1650; and Upper Xingu settlements inhabited until about 1770, their circular-plaza layouts matching the villages living Kuikuro communities build today]{claim=AMZ-C011}. That last point deserves its own sentence: some of this is not a lost world at all, but a continuous one — collapsed in numbers, unbroken in pattern. The caution is geographic: Santarém, Marajó, and the Xingu are the lower Amazon and its southern tributaries, not the Machiparo and Omagua reaches where Carvajal's most famous passages sit.

## Engineered ground

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P03}

The subsistence question — *what could they all have eaten?* — was always the strongest scientific objection, and it now has at least one direct answer. [In the Llanos de Mojos, the Casarabe culture ran intensive year-round maize agriculture on a savannah it had replumbed: drainage canals for the wet season, farm ponds for the dry, documented by phytoliths in the fields themselves]{claim=AMZ-C007}. More broadly, [dark earths, raised-field complexes, forest islands, and orchard-like concentrations of domesticated trees around archaeological sites record long human engineering of Amazonian ground]{claim=AMZ-C008}.

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P04}

The savannah's waters were engineered too, and “they couldn't have gotten enough protein” was for decades the respectable core of the impossibility argument. Here the record is uneven in an instructive way. The paper on the San Joaquín floodplains reports [zigzag weirs and straight causeways crossing the savanna, most of the hundreds of detected ponds within thirty-five meters of one, and postulates that the V-shaped structures served to concentrate fish as the floods receded]{claim=AMZ-C019} — but this ledger holds that only on the paper's anchor; no evidence record from it has yet been admitted, and the claim is graded accordingly. The diet, by contrast, is in the ground and in the record: [one settlement's refuse holds more than seventeen thousand fish bones, including dry-season species like lungfish that persist in small waters — year-round aquatic harvest, fifty kilometers from the big river]{claim=AMZ-C026}. One site's refuse is an existence proof, not a census. But the specific claim the old skepticism rested on — that the interfluves could not feed sedentary people through the year — now has a documented counterexample in bone, and in maize. Note the calendar: the Casarabe world ends around 1400, a century and a half before Orellana. It answers the impossibility argument; it does not describe 1542.

Engineering is not a census, and this case keeps the distinction structural. [The raised fields of the Bolivian lowlands, dated carefully, show intermittent construction and use — plausibly flood-risk works built where nothing else would do — not a permanent breadbasket]{claim=AMZ-C009}. And the domesticated-forest signal carries a first-class qualifier: five post-Columbian centuries have shaped the modern forest too, and the formal critique arguing they did most of the shaping is part of this record. A second study finds that [across 1,676 forest plots, 53 of 79 domesticated tree species track the modelled probability that earthworks are present]{claim=AMZ-C033} — corroboration, but from inside the same research network, using the same species list, and open to the same post-Columbian confound. The record counts it once, not twice.

## How many people?

The honest answer to the famous question is that the published numbers — one million, five, six, ten — are not competing measurements. They are competing models, and several descend from the same assumptions. The field's most influential estimator said so himself: [Denevan publicly rejected the habitat-density method behind his own 5.1–6.8 million figure, while still judging “at least 5 to 6 million” reasonable on other grounds]{claim=AMZ-C012}. A number can outlive the death of the argument that produced it; a reader deserves to know when that has happened.

What the aggregate evidence does support: [radiocarbon proxies for the whole biome fit a population growing logistically toward carrying capacity right up to European arrival]{claim=AMZ-C015} — no sign, at basin scale, that Amazonian societies were already dying out on their own before the caravels. The authors' own caveats govern: the proxy tracks relative change, its terminal dip is attributed to sampling bias compounded by post-contact collapse, and “carrying capacity (however high)” says nothing about how high.

## The disappearance

If Carvajal described a real world, where did it go? The documented answer, where colonial records permit counting, is brutal and specific. [In the Napo–Aguarico province, an estimated 49,000–51,000 people in the early contact period became about 6,000 by 1700 — an 88 percent collapse; neighboring Mainas lost roughly two-thirds — through differing regional mixtures of epidemics, slave raids, missionization, forced labor, revolt, and flight]{claim=AMZ-C010}. Note the mechanism list: people did not only die in place. They were taken, gathered into missions, and they fled — most, the record says, from exposed locations along the major rivers. The same paper is anchored here for a further proposition — that [in sparse lowlands epidemics commonly “faded out,” and it was the raids and the missions that kept reintroducing them]{claim=AMZ-C023} — which the ledger holds on that anchor alone, without an admitted evidence record; it is plausible and ungraded, not established. A riverbank empty in 1690 is not evidence it was empty in 1542; it may be evidence of everything that happened in between.

The limit is that these counts come from upper-Amazon provinces with mission records. The Solimões reaches where the dispute actually lives have no equivalent reconstruction, and the reconciliation argument borrows ratios from where the records are. The nearest thing to a mid-century count for Carvajal's Omagua reach — a Franciscan resident's headcount from around 1650 — survives in a 1900 edition whose printed numeral is garbled, and reading the manuscript behind it is one of this case's research items.

## The sparse Amazon

Everything above could be true and the maximalist picture still false, and the negative evidence is part of this case's spine, not an afterthought. [Across 7,363 recorded archaeological sites, distance from a river is the single strongest predictor of pre-Columbian occupation, with the deep interfluves markedly sparser]{claim=AMZ-C013}. And [where scientists have cored the soils of the western and interfluvial Amazon — fourteen regions and counting — most terra-firme profiles show closed-canopy forest with little to no sign of crops, clearing, dark earths, tree enrichment, or recurrent fire]{claim=AMZ-C014}. The skeptics of the garden Amazon are not defending the old impossibility thesis; they are defending proportions. Two modelling papers are anchored here for that position — one reckoning [the famous earthworks and dark earths cover a “limited, albeit impressive” fraction, with humbler site types dominating more than two-thirds of the basin]{claim=AMZ-C020}, the other reported as putting [almost 80 percent of Amazonia at a 0–1 percent chance of holding an earthwork in any given square kilometer, the low-probability country concentrated in the northwest, north, and center]{claim=AMZ-C029} — and both are held on their anchors alone, with no evidence record admitted from either; the ledger knows where the propositions are stated and grades them unresolved until it holds the observation behind them.

The negatives have their own critics, and here too the ledger holds statements rather than records. A formal reply argues that [the “sparse west” rests on some three hundred soil cores in five clusters — about a cubic meter of sediment standing in for two million square kilometers]{claim=AMZ-C021}; a palaeoecological study of the Upano Valley in Ecuador reports that [forest recovery largely erased the pre-Columbian signal even though the later colonial signal survived]{claim=AMZ-C022}, so that a negative would mean less the older the activity. Both are anchor-only in this record. What the record does hold is the Upano chronology from the excavating team: [the Kilamope/Upano occupation ran from about 500 BCE to between 300 and 600 CE]{claim=AMZ-C061}, [it was groups of those two cultures that built the platforms and roads]{claim=AMZ-C086}, and [some mounds were reoccupied between 800 and 1200 CE]{claim=AMZ-C062}. The erased signal, in other words, was a thousand years old or more. Whether a signal four centuries old — the age of a riverbank depopulated in the 1600s — would also be gone is exactly what the erasure argument needs and does not yet have; a research item below proposes to measure the decay against sites with dated abandonments. And the site database that produces the river-distance gradient inherits the fact that archaeologists survey where they can reach. The case logs all of these biases rather than choosing one.

## What would decide it

Each live account makes a prediction the ledger can eventually check.

- **The corridor test.** Classify every reach of the 1541–42 route as populated or empty from the manuscripts alone, model the route's uncertainty, then compare contact-horizon (AD 1400–1650) archaeology in his populated reaches against matched controls. The murdered-world and mosaic readings predict a strong match; the modest skeptic predicts that his populated reaches are real but no denser than other bluff-and-channel settings; invention predicts nothing there at all.
- **The witness table.** A passage-by-passage collation of the manuscript branches, now including which passages Oviedo owed to Orellana's oral account rather than the friar's pen. If the qualitative bedrock turns out to be branch-specific too, Carvajal's rehabilitation weakens; if only the figures are, it hardens — and the collation would show which way the figures moved.
- **Promise-blind surveys.** LiDAR and gridded coring across interfluvial blocks chosen without regard to archaeological promise, with controls for whether the method could have detected occupation. The garden Amazon predicts interfluve densities approaching riverine ones; the mosaic predicts a real but low matrix; the modest skeptic predicts near-zero outside a few hotspots.
- **The 1650 headcount.** Read the Biblioteca Nacional manuscript behind the garbled 1900 edition to fix how many men a resident friar found on the Omagua reach a century after Carvajal. Tens or hundreds would mean the corridor was near-empty by mid-century, a dated witness for the murdered world; low thousands would mean a province of a thousand or more households still standing in 1650, moving the collapse's timing and size.
- **Erasure calibration.** Score anthropogenic indicators in soil profiles beside sites with archaeologically fixed end dates — Upano, Casarabe, Belterra, Marajó, the Xingu — and plot signal against years since abandonment. If four-century-old signals survive while Upano's millennium-old one is gone, the erasure argument cannot discount contact-era negatives.
- **Stratified LiDAR.** Survey blocks drawn at random within probability strata of the two earthwork models, to see which total is calibrated.
- **Dependency-corrected demography.** Sort every published estimate into its model family and re-derive them under one assumption set, so model families stop masquerading as independent censuses.
- **Middle-Amazon collapse timelines.** Extend province-by-province reconstruction to the Solimões, testing whether documented decline and relocation suffice to turn 1542 into the later silence.

## Where this case lands

[The pre-contact Amazon that survives every filter in this record is a strongly heterogeneous one: substantial populations, engineered subsistence, and settlement systems along favored corridors and hotspots, embedded in a much more lightly occupied forest matrix]{claim=AMZ-C016}. This is a synthesis, not an observation — it carries no evidence record of its own and stands on the corridor archaeology and the river-distance gradient beneath it. Neither the pristine wilderness nor the wall-to-wall civilization survives contact with the evidence; what remains open is proportions, and “heterogeneous” only earns its keep once the matrix density is measured rather than inferred.

How connected was this world? The ledger holds, on its anchor, a linguist's boundary: [regional interaction spheres are well documented — shared ceramic traditions, exchange, stable multilingualism — while the strong version, a continent-spanning Arawak-dominated integration, is assessed as resting on “quite weak” evidence]{claim=AMZ-C025}, a criticism its author limits to the strong version. That is the mosaic again, at the level of politics and language.

And the friar? [Carvajal now looks substantially credible about the qualitative social geography he described, and untrustworthy about his extreme numbers]{claim=AMZ-C017} — a more interesting vindication than the wholesale kind, because it is earned by discounting everything discountable and testing what is left. It is also provisional. The corroboration comes from the same corridors and the same genre of conquest narrative; the contemporary endorsements are of his character, not his counts; the contact-horizon settlement systems dated so far lie downstream and to the south of his most famous passages; and the test that would close the question has not been run.

## Credit where the record supports it

One more genealogical fact belongs in the open. [Years before the 2026 results, Graham Hancock's *America Before* devoted seven chapters to the Amazonian discoveries — the Acre geoglyphs among them — and his 2024 series put Pärssinen and Ranzi themselves in front of a mass audience]{claim=AMZ-C018}, at a time when this research was marginal to the mainstream conversation. On this site, outsider status is not evidence — in either direction. Hancock's larger lost-civilization thesis is not what this evidence establishes, and the mainstream's numerical skepticism about Carvajal has been partly vindicated by the manuscript work. But a truthful genealogy records who kept the question alive while the instruments were catching up, and this is such a record.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis graded is the heterogeneous one: substantial sedentary populations, engineered subsistence and settlement systems along favored corridors and hotspots, set in a much more lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively credible and numerically unreliable. Admitted records carry it from both directions. Positively: earthworks at enormous scale in the Aquiry region (AMZ-E001 on C004); fortified southern-rim villages dated AD 1250–1500 (AMZ-E004 on C006); settlement systems occupied into the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries at Santarém, Marajó and the Xingu (AMZ-E017, E018, E019 on C011); engineered year-round maize on the Casarabe savanna (AMZ-E014 on C007) and a year-round interfluvial fish diet at Loma Salvatierra (AMZ-E022 on C026), exactly where the carrying-capacity objection was strongest; and independent 1538 and 1560 witnesses converging on the same middle-Amazon reaches Carvajal described (AMZ-E007 on C003), with the chronicle's extreme figures shown to be branch-specific (AMZ-E005 on C002). Negatively: the river-distance gradient across 7,363 sites (AMZ-E010 on C013) and the thin intensive-use signal in fourteen sampled regions (AMZ-E011 on C014) cap the garden-Amazon reading. Demography stays a set of assumption-driven envelopes (AMZ-E002 on C005; AMZ-E009 on C012); the basin-wide comparator records (AMZ-E038, E039 on C004) show earthwork totals differing several-fold between models; the tree-species corroboration (AMZ-E040, E041 on C008 and C033) comes from one research network and counts once, under the post-Columbian confound AMZ-E013 states. Six featured limits claims — the fisheries infrastructure (C019), the site-type and probability-surface modelling (C020, C029), the soil-core sampling critique (C021), the Upano erasure (C022) and the epidemic fade-out mechanism (C023) — are held on anchors with no admitted evidence record and are graded unresolved; the qualifiers that would keep the negatives from being read as proof of emptiness are therefore statements, not records, and the lightly-occupied half of the thesis rests on E010 and E011 with the limitations those records themselves state. The Upano chronology carried on its own claims — occupation 500 BCE to 300/600 CE (AMZ-E073 on C061), building by Kilamope and Upano groups (AMZ-E115 on C086), Huapula reoccupation to 1200 CE (AMZ-E074 on C062) — is relevant to C022 only by inference: if the erasure claim is ever admitted, the signal it says was erased was a millennium old, not the four-century-old signal of a riverbank depopulated in the 1600s; AMZ-R008 is the test. The Medina 1894 records on the chronicle change how the textual leg is read without changing its grade: Oviedo's statement that he supplemented the friar's text orally from Orellana and his companions (AMZ-E089 on C074) means the two manuscript branches are not independent witnesses, so E005 establishes that the figures are unstable but not which way they moved; the earliest lie-charge, Gómara's 'mentirosa', targeted Orellana's relación (AMZ-E080 on C068) and, on Medina's reading, the Amazons episode (AMZ-E082 on C069; AMZ-E099, E100 as context on C017), not the populous settlements; Herrera follows Carvajal almost to the letter (AMZ-E093 on C077), so later Spanish narratives are redactions, not corroboration; and the contemporary endorsements — Oviedo's two arrow wounds and reported reputation (AMZ-E113 on C072, E114 on C085, E105 and E106 as context on C017), the friar's truth-oath (AMZ-E091 on C075), Medina's 'complete faith' limited to voyage events with caveats for supernatural attribution and partisanship for Orellana (AMZ-E109, E110, E111 on C017; E112 on C076) — are credibility of the witness, not tests of content, and add no diagnostic weight. Achmatowicz's geographic-route assessment (AMZ-E072 on C065; E077 as context on C017) converges with C017 but is abstract-only and silent on the qualitative-versus-numerical split. The synthesis claims are graded on disclosed bases, not on anchors: C016 on the records attached to its dependency claims (E001, E004, E014, E017–E019, E010, E011), C017 on E007 and E005 through its dependencies, with E003 (on C004 and C017) marking that the Aquiry peak is a millennium too early to speak for 1542. Neither invention nor pristine wilderness survives the record; what it cannot yet fix is the matrix density that separates the mosaic from the modest skeptic, or contact-horizon archaeology on Carvajal's own reaches. Sensitivity: the single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is AMZ-E007. Without it the Carvajal leg (C017) falls to weakly supported — every remaining corroboration is archaeological, off his route, earlier than him, or about his character — and the founding question's verdict would fall to provisionally supported even though the archaeological mosaic (C016) would stand. On the matrix side AMZ-E010 plays the equivalent role: without it the lightly occupied half rests on the fourteen-region synthesis alone.
assessment.steelman: Every witness who saw the middle Amazon before the epidemics — Nunes in 1538, Carvajal in 1542, the ten Ursúa chroniclers in 1560 — reports the same specific, unglamorous features on the same reaches: stores of maize, long straight roads compared to Inca roads without walls, ceramics of known reputation, dense settlement (AMZ-E007). These witnesses wrote for different crowns and, on the admitted reading, did not copy one another; convergence on mundane detail is what shared exaggeration does not produce, and the one feature that does not converge — the giant warrior counts — is exactly the feature the manuscript branches show to be unstable (AMZ-E005). Proponents read that pattern as the signature of a truthful observer whose numbers moved in transmission; they note that the 1894 editor who collated the branches judged the chronicle, limited to the events of the voyage, worthy of complete faith (AMZ-E109), and that the earliest charge of lying, Gómara's, was aimed at the captain's narrative (AMZ-E080) and, on Medina's reading, at the Amazons (AMZ-E099), never at the towns — so the invention account, on their reading, was born from a marvel and later transferred to the settlements without new grounds. A scholar working from a different direction, testing the chronicle's geographic reference points and league distances against the river, reads the manuscript as a trustworthy source (AMZ-E072); proponents take that as an independent check on the friar's honesty, though this ledger has read only the abstract. Nothing admitted contradicts the witnesses where they stood: the negative palaeoecology (AMZ-E011) is from interfluves and the west, not from the Solimões bluffs, and Denevan's own bluff model (AMZ-E006) predicts the alternation of dense and empty reaches the friar reports. Where colonial records permit counting, decline of 62–88 percent within a century and a half is documented, by mechanisms — flight from exposed river locations, gathering into missions, slave raids — that empty riverbanks specifically (AMZ-E008); every lower-Amazon settlement system dated so far runs into the seventeenth century or later (AMZ-E017, E018, E019); and the basin-wide radiocarbon proxy grows to the eve of contact with no endogenous crash (AMZ-E020). On this argument the burden lies on the skeptic to explain why corridor eyewitnesses should be discounted when nothing contradicts them where they stood, and this assessment has no record that does so; it holds Carvajal at provisionally supported only because the direct corridor test has not been run, the dated contact-era systems lie off his route, and the manuscript branches have not yet been collated to show which way the figures moved.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: That Gaspar de Carvajal's 1542 chronicle describes a real world — populous, organized, road-connected riverine societies along specific reaches of the Amazon; that Amazonian environments could and did support large sedentary populations with engineered subsistence, at scales admitted evidence shows for LiDAR-documented earthworks, dark earths, raised fields, drainage canals and farm ponds — and, held here on its anchor only, landscape-scale fish weirs; and that Old World epidemics, slave raiding, missionization and flight destroyed and dispersed that world fast enough that the emptier Amazon met by later travelers records a collapse rather than proving the earlier account false. The version this assessment grades is the heterogeneous one: dense corridors and hotspots embedded in a lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively credible and his extreme numbers a transmission artefact whose direction of travel between the manuscript branches is not yet fixed.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether complex Amazonian societies existed — earthworks, dark earths, engineered savannas and planned settlements are established beyond argument. The live cruxes are proportion and inference. How representative were the populated corridors of the basin, when river distance is the dominant predictor of known occupation and most sampled interfluves show little intensive modification — while the critiques of that negative sampling, and the erasure argument that would discount it, are held in this ledger on anchors without admitted records? Do population estimates survive their own assumptions, when the largest recent figure falls roughly fivefold under the paper's own alternative reading, the field's most influential estimator rejected his own method, and earthwork totals differ several-fold between predictive models? How much of Carvajal is textual bedrock versus transmission artefact, when the most famous warrior counts sit in one manuscript branch only and the other branch was, by its compiler's own statement, supplemented from Orellana's mouth? And are spectacular but much earlier or geographically distant sites — the Aquiry peak of AD 100–300, Upano ending by 600 CE, the Casarabe world ending around 1400, the lower-Amazon systems — being silently spent as evidence about the reaches Carvajal saw in 1542?
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A preregistered Carvajal corridor test: classify his populated and empty reaches from the manuscript witnesses alone, model route and palaeochannel uncertainty, then compare contact-horizon archaeological intensity in his populated corridors against matched controls — before consulting the archaeological layers. Alongside it: a synoptic manuscript-witness table separating what every Carvajal branch shares from what one branch carries, and marking which Oviedo passages derive from Orellana's oral account; promise-blind interfluve surveys with proxy-sensitivity controls to measure the matrix density directly; the Biblioteca Nacional manuscript reading that fixes the 1650 Omagua headcount; an erasure-decay calibration against sites with dated abandonments, so the Upano argument stops standing in for four-century-old signals; a probability-stratified blind LiDAR sample to calibrate the competing earthwork totals; demographic estimates re-derived under a common assumption set; and province-by-province collapse timelines extended to the Solimões.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: The modern skeptical position is not the old ecological-impossibility argument; it concedes major regional societies and argues limits. Orellana travelled the richest corridors — the bluff-and-channel settings where settlement concentrated and where archaeology preferentially looks and preserves — so corroboration there cannot license basin-wide extrapolation. Sampled western and interfluvial palaeoecology shows large areas without intensive cultivation, clearing or soil modification, and the predictive-modelling papers this ledger holds on their anchors state that the spectacular earthworks and dark earths are a limited, if impressive, fraction of the basin. The famous population totals are model outputs whose assumptions — site contemporaneity, persons per earthwork, extrapolation domains — do most of the work, and the estimators themselves have said so. Carvajal's extreme figures are textually unstable across manuscript branches that are not independent of one another, consistent with a truthful observer whose numbers changed in the telling; his contemporary endorsements are of his character, not his counts. On this view the mosaic is real but modest: dense hotspots, thin matrix, and a chronicle that is qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable, describing a world that was both smaller than legend and then genuinely destroyed.

components.label: The chronicle: text, transmission and independent witnesses
components.note: The chronicle's qualitative picture is corroborated by witnesses of 1538 and 1560 on the same reaches (AMZ-E007 on C003); its extreme figures are branch-specific (AMZ-E005 on C002) but the branches are not independent (AMZ-E089 on C074), so direction of change is open. The earliest lie-charge targeted Orellana's relación (AMZ-E080 on C068); character endorsements (E105, E106, E113, E114, E091) carry no diagnostic weight. The attribution that Carvajal is credible in kind and unreliable in number (C017) is provisional pending the corridor test.

components.label: Earthworks and contact-era settlement systems
components.note: Aquiry earthworks at scale (AMZ-E001 on C004), dated a millennium before Orellana (E003); southern-rim fortified villages AD 1250–1500 (AMZ-E004 on C006); Santarém, Marajó and Xingu systems running into the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (E017, E018, E019 on C011); Upano dated 500 BCE–300/600 CE (E073 on C061). The contact-era systems lie off Carvajal's most famous reaches.

components.label: Engineered subsistence
components.note: Year-round maize monoculture on engineered savanna (AMZ-E014 on C007); year-round interfluvial fishing in bone (AMZ-E022 on C026); dark earths, raised fields and domesticated-tree concentrations (E012, E040, E041 on C008), qualified by the post-Columbian confound (E013) and by intermittent raised-field use (E015, E016 on C009). The weir infrastructure (C019) is anchor-only and unresolved.

components.label: Population totals
components.note: The finding is that the numbers are model envelopes, not measurements: the Aquiry headline spans roughly fivefold under the paper's own alternative (AMZ-E002 on C005); Denevan rejected the method behind his own figure while keeping the magnitude (AMZ-E009 on C012); the radiocarbon proxy shows growth to contact but not a level (AMZ-E020 on C015). No admitted record fixes a basin total.

components.label: The lightly occupied matrix
components.note: River distance dominates occupation across 7,363 sites (AMZ-E010 on C013) and fourteen sampled regions show little intensive-use signal (AMZ-E011 on C014), with the survey-effort and proxy-sensitivity limits those records state. The modelling claims (C020, C029), the sampling critique (C021) and the erasure claim (C022) are anchor-only and graded unresolved; the matrix density itself is unmeasured.

components.label: The disappearance
components.note: Documented decline of 88% (Napo–Aguarico) and 62–64% (Mainas) by about 1700 through epidemics, raids, missionization, revolt and flight from exposed river locations (AMZ-E008 on C010), from upper-Amazon provinces with mission records. The fade-out mechanism (C023) is anchor-only; no equivalent reconstruction exists for the Solimões reaches Carvajal described.

researchPriority.reason: Two desk items (the corridor test, AMZ-R001; the manuscript-witness table, AMZ-R002) and one archival reading (AMZ-R007) can be run without fieldwork and would decide the claims this case holds at provisionally supported or unresolved — Carvajal's representativeness, the direction of the figures' drift, and the 1650 Omagua headcount — while promise-blind surveys (AMZ-R003, R006) and the erasure calibration (AMZ-R008) are the only way to measure the matrix density that separates the mosaic from the modest skeptic.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim states what the chronicle contains, and its content is fixed by the manuscript comparison and verbatim quotations the anchor names and by the records on its child claims: AMZ-E005 (on C002) confirms the populous-settlement picture is present in both branches, and AMZ-E007 (on C003) confirms the same features on the same reaches. AMZ-E006 (attached here) qualifies the reading by placing the alternation of dense and empty reaches within Denevan's bluff model, which is what the claim's final clause records. Disclosed basis: E005 and E007 via the dependency claims.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvajal's 1542 account really does describe crowded, organized riverbank societies with food stores, roads and fine pottery, broken by stretches he calls empty — that is what the text says, whatever the truth of it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: What the friar wrote is the case's starting point, not evidence for or against it; the claim defines the prediction the corridor test would check.
treatment.strongestObjection: A text's content is not its accuracy; the qualitative picture could be a genre convention shared by conquest narratives seeking patronage.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A manuscript collation (AMZ-R002) showing that the populous-settlement descriptions are themselves branch-specific rather than shared bedrock.
Evidence that the empty-stretch reports were later insertions or editorial rationalizations.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E005 (strong, supports) quotes Denevan's branch comparison verbatim: the 50,000, 10,000 and 8,000 figures and the four- and five-league villages are in the Medina/Muñoz versions and absent from Oviedo's, which has one figure of about 5,000. The limitation is that the comparison was verified from an OCR copy and is a geographer's, not a philologist's collation; a blocked attempt to place each figure by witness at page level remains open.

treatment.plainLanguage: The huge warrior counts live in one family of copies only; the other version keeps the crowded world but drops the giant numbers.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Splits the chronicle into a shared qualitative core and a branch-specific numerical layer, which is what lets the case grade Carvajal in kind and in number separately — though AMZ-E089 (on C074) shows the branches are not independent, so the split shows instability, not direction.
treatment.strongestObjection: If Oviedo trimmed the figures on his own authority or from Orellana's account, their absence from his version says nothing about what the friar originally wrote.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A page-level collation (AMZ-R002) placing the figures by witness and showing them present in every branch.
Evidence that Oviedo edited the numbers down rather than inheriting a text without them.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E089 (strong, supports) quotes Oviedo through Medina: beyond the friar's eyewitness text, he learned particulars in Santo Domingo from Orellana and other gentlemen who came with him. Confidence is moderate because Oviedo is quoted at second hand; the Oviedo volume itself is blocked in this ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: Oviedo says he added to the friar's written account what the captain and his companions told him in person — so his version is not a separate copy of the same text.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Undercuts the reading of the two branches as independent witnesses: where they differ, Orellana's oral account is a candidate source, so the branch comparison (C002) cannot by itself say which way the figures moved.
treatment.strongestObjection: Oviedo's supplement may concern narrative particulars rather than the passages carrying the figures; without the collation it is unknown which passages he touched.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading Oviedo's text directly and finding the supplemented passages marked or identifiable.
A collation showing the figure-bearing passages identical across branches except for the numbers.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E007 (strong, supports) quotes Lopes et al. 2024 on Nunes's 1538 entry into Machiparo and the ten Ursúa accounts of 1560, with the middle Solimões described as among the most densely inhabited areas, infinite maize stores, straight roads compared to Inca roads without walls, and renowned ceramics. Limitations stated on the record: Nunes survives as a 1553/54 letter through a modern edition; fortifications and organized warfare are not among the shared features.

treatment.plainLanguage: Other Europeans who saw the same stretch of river before and after Carvajal described the same crowded, road-connected world — without his giant numbers.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The record that decides against invention: independent witnesses for different crowns converge on mundane features on the same reaches. It does not decide the numbers or the representativeness of those reaches.
treatment.strongestObjection: All witnesses travelled the same corridor with the same expectations of rich provinces, and conquest narratives share tropes; convergence on a corridor is not convergence on the basin.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the primary Nunes letter and Ursúa accounts and finding the shared features to be later editorial harmonization.
Contact-horizon archaeology on the Machiparo–Omagua reaches (AMZ-R001) showing no dense settlement.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E080 (moderate, supports) quotes Medina: Gómara cited Orellana's relación and called it 'mentirosa', without stating grounds. Gómara's own text is not in the ledger; the grade rests on Medina's report.

treatment.plainLanguage: The first recorded accusation of lying was aimed at the captain's own report of the voyage, not at the friar's chronicle.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Locates the origin of the invention account; it says nothing about whether the settlements were real.
treatment.strongestObjection: Gómara may have known Orellana's relación only through material shared with Carvajal's, so the charge could reach the friar's text indirectly.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading Gómara's 1552 passage in context and finding the charge directed at the settlement descriptions.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E072 (weak, supports) is the article's abstract only: it says the manuscript can be considered a trustworthy source after a study of its geographic reference points. The body, its route argument and any treatment of the figures were not read.

treatment.plainLanguage: A 2018 scholar checked the chronicle's geography against the river and judged it trustworthy — but this ledger has read only the abstract.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A convergent scholarly opinion reached by a different route; geographic plausibility does not test the population descriptions or the counts.
treatment.strongestObjection: A geographically coherent itinerary is compatible with an exaggerated or invented social picture; the abstract does not address the figures.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the article body and finding its geographic checks do or do not extend to the populated reaches.
A route reconstruction contradicting the chronicle's league distances.

claimAssessments.reasoning: This synthesis claim has no supporting record of its own; its nine attached records are context or weak qualifiers. Disclosed basis: AMZ-E007 (on C003) for independent corroboration of the qualitative picture and AMZ-E005 (on C002) for the instability of the extreme figures. AMZ-E003 (attached) qualifies by dating the Aquiry peak a millennium before Orellana; AMZ-E111 qualifies by noting the friar's partisanship for Orellana; E077, E099, E100, E105, E106, E109, E110 are context on genealogy and character and add no diagnostic weight. Off-route contact-era systems (E017–E019 on C011) and the southern rim (E004 on C006) show the kind of world was possible but do not sit on his reaches.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvajal looks honest about the kind of world he saw and unreliable about how many people were in it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the case's answer to its founding question; if it stands, invention fails and the murdered-world and mosaic readings stay live, with proportion the remaining dispute.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every corroboration is from the same corridors and the same conquest-narrative genre, the contemporary endorsements are of character not content, and the dated contact-era archaeology lies off his route; the qualitative picture has not yet been tested where he stood.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The preregistered corridor test (AMZ-R001) finding contact-horizon archaeology no denser in his populated reaches than in matched controls.
The manuscript collation (AMZ-R002) showing the populous-settlement descriptions are themselves branch-specific.
The 1650 Omagua headcount (AMZ-R007) in the low thousands, favouring a modest reality over a large collapse.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E001 (strong, supports) gives the 432 earthworks from 10 LiDAR lines, the 183,000 km² circumscription and the 24,000–30,000 projection verbatim; AMZ-E003 (strong, qualifies) dates the demographic peak to AD 100–300; AMZ-E038 and E039 (context) show a basin-wide 2023 model predicting fewer undiscovered earthworks for all Amazonia than the 2026 study projects for one region, with different definitions and data. The projection is a block extrapolation, as the record states. Funding by this site's founder is disclosed on the source.

treatment.plainLanguage: Laser survey under the canopy found hundreds of earthworks and projects tens of thousands across one southwestern region — built mostly a thousand-plus years before Orellana.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decisive against the claim that Amazonian environments could not carry monument-building societies; weak about 1542, because the peak is a millennium earlier and the region is off Carvajal's route.
treatment.strongestObjection: The regional projection exceeds a basin-wide model's total several-fold, and the site count is a sampled-density extrapolation not yet tested blind (AMZ-R006).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A probability-stratified blind LiDAR sample (AMZ-R006) finding densities far below the 2026 projection.
Redating showing the earthworks span into the contact era, which would raise their relevance to 1542.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E002 (strong, supports) quotes the paper's own derivation — 25–60% simultaneous use, 300 people per earthwork — and its single-family alternative of 250,000–600,000 (315,000–760,000 with canopy correction). The authors label the alternative very unlikely; the sensitivity is theirs, the emphasis the case's.

treatment.plainLanguage: The headline of one to three million people depends on two assumptions; change one and the paper's own numbers fall roughly fivefold.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shows that even the best-documented regional total is an assumption envelope, which caps what any population figure can do for the garden-Amazon account.
treatment.strongestObjection: The authors give reasons for preferring the higher assumptions; displaying the span as the error bar may understate the case for the headline.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: House-floor excavation data fixing persons per earthwork independently of ethnographic analogy.
Radiocarbon programs fixing the simultaneous-use fraction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E004 (strong, supports) states the 1,800 km occupation by fortified villages at cal AD 1250–1500 and reproduces the population model with its stated assumptions of site contemporaneity, ethnographic formulae and MaxEnt projection. The occupation finding is well supported; the population range is a model, as the claim says.

treatment.plainLanguage: Along the southern edge of the Amazon, fortified earth-built villages were occupied in the centuries just before European contact; the half-million-to-a-million estimate is a model with named assumptions.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Contact-adjacent settlement at regional scale supports the mosaic and murdered-world readings, but the southern rim is not Carvajal's river and the count is not a measurement.
treatment.strongestObjection: The end date of 1500 leaves open whether these villages were still occupied in 1542, and contemporaneity is assumed rather than shown.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Site-by-site dating showing sequential rather than contemporaneous occupation.
Dependency-corrected re-derivation (AMZ-R004) collapsing the population range.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E017 (strong) dates Belterra Plateau sites ca. AD 1300 to seventeenth-century colonization with dark earths, ponds and trodden roads; AMZ-E018 (strong) dates Marajó's Cacoal to AD 1300–1650 into Portuguese contact; AMZ-E019 (moderate, journalism) gives Upper Xingu occupation 500–1770 CE in layouts matching living Kuikuro villages. The Xingu leg is held at secondary-source weight pending primary reports.

treatment.plainLanguage: Several large settlement systems were still inhabited when Europeans arrived, and one of them is continuous with villages people build today.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Directly supports the murdered-world mechanism — populous systems existed at contact and then shrank — and refutes the pristine-wilderness reading; its limit is geographic, since none of these lie on the Machiparo–Omagua reaches.
treatment.strongestObjection: Lower-Amazon and southern-tributary systems say nothing about the middle Solimões where Carvajal's famous passages sit; the Xingu leg rests on a news feature.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Primary Xingu excavation reports failing to sustain the dating or layout claims.
Contact-horizon dating on Carvajal's own reaches (AMZ-R001) showing no equivalent systems.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E073 (strong, supports) quotes the excavating team's dating of the Upano occupation from around 500 BCE to between 300 and 600 CE, on almost seventy radiocarbon dates per the supplement; the author-accepted manuscript promises a revised sequence.

treatment.plainLanguage: The Upano Valley's platform-building society ended roughly a thousand years before Carvajal.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Low for the thesis itself, but it fixes the age of the signal the Upano erasure argument (C022) says was lost — a millennium old, not four centuries — which is what AMZ-R008 must calibrate.
treatment.strongestObjection: The dating sequence is under revision by its own authors.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The promised revised chronology moving the end of occupation substantially later.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E014 (strong, supports) quotes the drainage canals, farm ponds and the maize phytoliths in 178 samples from 18 soil profiles, with the authors' conclusion of intensive year-round maize monoculture. The record notes the Casarabe florescence (500–1400 CE) ends before contact.

treatment.plainLanguage: One Bolivian savanna society re-plumbed its landscape to grow maize all year — a direct answer to the claim that the Amazon could not feed sedentary populations.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Refutes the ecological-impossibility premise behind the invention account; it does not describe 1542, because the Casarabe world ended around 1400.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single savanna culture with unusual hydrology is not a template for forested riverbanks a thousand kilometres away.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Phytolith reanalysis showing maize confined to a few profiles or seasons.
Redating showing the hydraulic system postdates the occupation.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E012 (moderate, supports) gives the Levis et al. finding that domesticated species concentrate on and around archaeological sites; AMZ-E040 and E041 (moderate, supports) find 53 of 79 domesticated species associated with modelled earthwork probability, from the same research network and species list; AMZ-E013 (moderate, qualifies) argues post-Columbian activity likely shaped the floristic pattern more than pre-Columbian. Dark earths are documented on C011's records (E017) and raised fields on C009's (E015, E016). The landscape-engineering leg is established; the tree leg carries a live confound.

treatment.plainLanguage: Human-made soils, field systems, forest islands and orchard-like tree concentrations show people reshaped Amazonian ground over long periods.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Supports the engineered-corridor half of the mosaic; the tree-composition signal cannot separate pre- from post-Columbian management, so it counts once and weakly for the pre-contact scale.
treatment.strongestObjection: Five post-Columbian centuries of settlement and trade also concentrate useful trees near old sites; the modern forest may record the colonial era more than the pre-Columbian one.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dated palaeoecological cores separating pre- and post-Columbian enrichment near sites.
Independent groups with different species lists failing to replicate the association.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E015 (moderate, supports) proposes raised fields as flood-risk mitigation built where no alternatives existed; AMZ-E016 (strong, supports) dates intermittent use from AD 570–770 in a few construction events, challenging continuous cultivation. Bermeo-area fields specifically; other complexes may differ.

treatment.plainLanguage: The raised fields were built in bursts and used intermittently, probably against floods — not farmed continuously as a permanent breadbasket.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Cuts against the garden-Amazon reading of raised fields as evidence of intensive continuous agriculture, while leaving engineered subsistence intact.
treatment.strongestObjection: Intermittent dating at one complex does not show intermittent use everywhere; the Casarabe maize system (C007) shows continuous intensification elsewhere in the same region.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dating at other raised-field complexes showing continuous construction and use.
Phytolith evidence of sustained cropping on the Bermeo fields.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: no admitted evidence record from the Blatrix et al. paper exists in this ledger. The proposition is what the paper states, not what the case shows.

treatment.plainLanguage: A published study reports fish weirs and causeways across a Bolivian floodplain, with ponds clustered beside them — but this record has not yet admitted the observation behind it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, landscape-scale fisheries would strengthen the engineered-subsistence leg against the protein-scarcity argument; until then the claim contributes nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: The function of the V-shaped structures is postulated, and the paper itself notes they concentrate fish less intensely than modern analogues.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of evidence records from the source stating the weir count, pond proximity and functional inference.
Excavation or ethnographic analogy confirming the structures' function.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E022 (strong, supports) quotes the more than 17,000 fish remains at Loma Salvatierra, 50 km from the Mamoré, occupied 500–1400 AD, demonstrating year-round resources, with lungfish and tiger-fish named as dry-season species. The source's own caveat: few large river fish, suggesting infrequent exogenous contributions.

treatment.plainLanguage: One interfluvial mound's refuse proves people there ate fish all year, including dry-season species from small waters.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An existence proof against the protein-scarcity form of the impossibility argument; one site is not a census and the occupation ends before contact.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single monumental mound in a savanna with engineered ponds is a special case, not a measure of what ordinary interfluvial forest could sustain.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Zooarchaeology at other interfluvial sites showing seasonal gaps.
Reanalysis attributing the small-water species to wet-season floodplain catch.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E009 (decisive, supports) quotes Denevan's rejection of the habitat-density method behind his 5.1–6.8 million figure, with his continued belief that at least 5 to 6 million is reasonable.

treatment.plainLanguage: The most influential population estimate's own author disowned the method that produced it while keeping the number.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes that basin totals are model families, not measurements — the reason the case treats every headline number as an envelope and why the garden-Amazon account cannot rest on a total.
treatment.strongestObjection: Denevan's retained magnitude, reached on other grounds, may still be right; a failed method does not refute its output.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A dependency-corrected re-derivation (AMZ-R004) finding independent families converging on a narrow range.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E020 (moderate, supports) quotes the logistic fit over 1,700 years before colonization, the carrying-capacity inference 'however high', and the attribution of the terminal decline to sampling bias compounded by post-contact collapse. Summed date distributions are relative proxies with stated biases.

treatment.plainLanguage: Basin-wide radiocarbon dates suggest population was growing and levelling right up to European arrival, not already collapsing on its own.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Argues against a pre-European endogenous crash, which matters for the murdered-world reading; it fixes no level and so cannot separate the mosaic from the modest skeptic.
treatment.strongestObjection: Summed date distributions track dated sites, not people, and the terminal-decline attribution is the authors' interpretation of an ambiguous tail.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Regional date series showing declines well before contact in the corridors at issue.
Taphonomic or sampling models reproducing the logistic shape without demographic growth.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E008 (strong, supports) reproduces Newson's Table 1 — Napo–Aguarico 49,000–51,000 to 6,000 by about 1700, Mainas 62–64% decline — and the mixed mechanisms of epidemics, raids, missionization, forced service, revolt and flight from exposed river locations. The record's limit: upper-Amazon provinces with mission records.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where colonial records allow counting, populations fell by two-thirds to nine-tenths within a century and a half, and people fled the big rivers specifically.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Supplies the murdered-world mechanism with documented magnitudes and a riverbank-specific pattern; its geographic reach stops short of the Solimões reaches where the dispute lives.
treatment.strongestObjection: Mission-province ratios cannot be assumed to hold on the middle Amazon, and a decline of 88% from a modest base still leaves a modest 1542.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Province-by-province timelines for the Solimões (AMZ-R005) showing much smaller declines.
The 1650 Omagua headcount (AMZ-R007) implying a small pre-collapse population.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: no admitted evidence record supports the fade-out mechanism, and AMZ-E008 is attached to C010, not to this claim, so it cannot be spent here.

treatment.plainLanguage: The paper is anchored for the idea that epidemics in thin populations burned out and were re-seeded by raids and missions — a plausible mechanism this ledger has not yet admitted as evidence.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it would explain how a corridor could be emptied in stages over a century rather than in one wave; until then it is an ungraded statement.
treatment.strongestObjection: The mechanism is inferred from mission-province records and may not describe dense riverine populations where disease could sustain itself.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of an evidence record quoting the fade-out passage and its supporting cases.
Documented epidemic chronologies on the Solimões showing single-wave collapse.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E010 (strong, supports) quotes the 7,363-site model in which distance from river is the most important predictor (21.5% of permutation importance) and interfluvial areas are differentiated as more sparsely populated. Stated limit: site databases inherit survey-effort bias toward accessible riverine areas.

treatment.plainLanguage: Across thousands of known sites, being near a river is the best predictor of where people lived; the deep interior was sparser.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The strongest admitted record against the garden Amazon and for the matrix half of the mosaic; it cannot fix how sparse the matrix was because the site base is survey-biased.
treatment.strongestObjection: Archaeologists find sites where they can reach — along rivers — so a river gradient in known sites partly measures where people have looked.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind interfluve surveys (AMZ-R003) finding site densities approaching riverine ones.
Reanalysis with survey-effort covariates removing the gradient.

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E011 (strong, supports) quotes the cumulative fourteen-region synthesis: little to no evidence of annual crops, significant clearing, anthropic soils, tree enrichment or recurrent fires in most sampled terra firme. Stated limits: three regions of new fieldwork, spatially sparse coring, negatives count only where the proxy could detect the activity. The sampling critique (C021) and erasure argument (C022) that would discount it are anchor-only here.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where soils in the western and interior Amazon have been cored, most show closed forest with little sign of farming, clearing or human-made soil before Columbus.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Directly contradicts the garden-Amazon prediction of intensive-use signals nearly everywhere; it does not touch the riverine corridors and its negatives are bounded by proxy sensitivity and sampling.
treatment.strongestObjection: A few hundred cores in a handful of clusters stand for two million square kilometres, and forest recovery may erase old signals — both objections the ledger holds only as statements.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission and confirmation of the sampling critique (C021) with a spatial analysis showing the cores unrepresentative.
Erasure calibration (AMZ-R008) showing signals four centuries old are also lost.
Gridded coring (AMZ-R003) finding intensive-use signals in interfluvial blocks.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: no admitted evidence record from Walker et al. 2023 exists in this ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: A machine-learning paper is reported as finding earthworks and dark earths a limited if impressive fraction of the basin, with humbler site types dominating — a statement this ledger has not yet admitted as evidence.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it would give the modest-skeptic and mosaic readings a basin-scale proportion; until then it is ungraded.
treatment.strongestObjection: A prediction trained on known sites inherits their survey bias; 'other site types' may be under-recorded rather than dominant.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of evidence records quoting the predicted extents and their uncertainty.
Blind survey (AMZ-R006) contradicting the predicted proportions.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the Clement et al. reply is a verified source but no evidence record from it has been admitted.

treatment.plainLanguage: A formal reply argues that the sparse-west conclusion rests on about three hundred cores in five clusters — a criticism the ledger records as stated, not as shown.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted and sustained, it would weaken the negative palaeoecology (C014) as evidence of absence; until then it is an objection on record without weight.
treatment.strongestObjection: Thin sampling cuts both ways: it also means the positive record cannot license basin-wide claims, and the cores were placed to test specific hypotheses.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of an evidence record with the core count, cluster locations and the authors' response.
A spatial adequacy analysis of the coring program.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: no admitted evidence record from Bush et al. 2025 exists. The Upano chronology on C061, C062 and C086 (E073, E074, E115) is attached to those claims and bears on this one only by inference: the erased occupation ended by 300–600 CE with reoccupation to 1200 CE, so the signal at issue was a millennium old.

treatment.plainLanguage: An Upano Valley study reports that regrowing forest largely erased the ecological trace of a pre-Columbian occupation while a later colonial trace survived — a finding this ledger has not yet admitted as evidence.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it would grade palaeoecological negatives by age; but the Upano occupation was a thousand years old, so its erasure does not by itself discount negatives for riverbanks depopulated in the 1600s.
treatment.strongestObjection: Erasure of a millennium-old signal says nothing about four-century-old ones, and the colonial signal's persistence may reflect its different character rather than its youth.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of evidence records from the Upano study stating the erasure and the colonial persistence.
Erasure calibration (AMZ-R008) at sites abandoned around 1600–1770.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the attempted evidence record from Peripato et al. 2023 for the 80% low-probability figure failed verbatim verification and was refused; the admitted records from that source (E038, E039, E040, E041) are attached to C004, C008 and C033, not to this claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: The same basin-wide model is reported as putting most of Amazonia at near-zero probability of holding an earthwork — a figure this ledger has not yet verified in the text.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it would quantify the matrix for the modest-skeptic and mosaic readings; the probability-stratified LiDAR test (AMZ-R006) is designed around it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Low predicted earthwork probability is not low occupation probability; the model predicts one site type, and its low-probability regions are also its least surveyed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A verified evidence record quoting the 80% figure and its map.
Blind survey (AMZ-R006) finding earthworks in the 0–1% stratum.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A synthesis with no anchor and no record of its own; the grade is carried entirely by the disclosed basis of admitted records on its dependency claims: E001 (C004), E004 (C006), E014 (C007), E017–E019 (C011) for the dense corridors and hotspots, and E010 (C013), E011 (C014) for the lightly occupied matrix. Confidence is moderate because the matrix density is inferred from survey-biased sites and sparse cores, and the qualifiers that would bound it (C020, C021, C022, C029) are anchor-only.

treatment.plainLanguage: The pre-contact Amazon was neither empty nor uniformly full: dense engineered corridors and hotspots set in much emptier forest.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the case's own account; it excludes invention and the pristine wilderness on admitted records, and leaves the mosaic-versus-modest-skeptic proportion open.
treatment.strongestObjection: 'Heterogeneous' can describe any distribution; until the matrix density is measured rather than inferred, the claim is compatible with both a large and a modest total.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind interfluve surveys (AMZ-R003) finding either near-riverine densities (toward the garden Amazon) or near-zero (toward the modest skeptic).
Contact-horizon archaeology on Carvajal's reaches (AMZ-R001) failing to match his populated stretches.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The anchor is Hancock's first-party statement of seven chapters and more than 90 pages; AMZ-E021 (moderate, supports) records the 2024 series cast listing Pärssinen and Ranzi. The record itself states it carries no weight for any empirical claim about the Amazon.

treatment.plainLanguage: Graham Hancock wrote at length about the Acre geoglyphs in 2019 and put the LiDAR researchers on screen in 2024, before their 2026 paper.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Genealogy only: it records who publicized the research, and bears not at all on whether Carvajal's world existed or on Hancock's larger thesis.
treatment.strongestObjection: Popularizing a research program is not advancing it, and the mainstream skepticism Hancock opposed has been partly vindicated on the numbers.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Page-level reading of America Before showing the Amazon coverage smaller or different from the first-party statement.
